content: The recommendations and evidence assessments provided by the World Health Organization (WHO) regarding interventions to improve outcomes in preterm birth are based on a systematic review of available data. 1. Interventions to Improve Preterm Birth Outcomes: The evidence for many interventions is of low or very low quality, often due to wide confidence intervals crossing the line of no effect, small sample sizes, and design limitations in the studies contributing data. For some interventions, the estimated effects range from a small reduction to a significant increase in adverse outcomes, reflecting uncertainty in the evidence. 2. Betamimetics for Inhibiting Preterm Labour: The use of betamimetics shows a low-quality evidence base, with an estimated reduction of 2 fewer cases per 1,000 births (ranging from 16 fewer to 44 more). The importance of this intervention is considered critical, but the evidence is limited by design flaws and statistical heterogeneity. 3. Calcium Channel Blockers for Inhibiting Preterm Labour: Moderate-quality evidence suggests calcium channel blockers may have a beneficial effect, but the data is limited by statistical heterogeneity (I² > 60%) and small sample sizes. The confidence intervals cross the line of no effect, indicating uncertainty in the magnitude of the benefit. 4. Cyclo-Oxygenase (COX) Inhibitors for Inhibiting Preterm Labour: Low-quality evidence indicates an increase of 57 more cases per 1,000 births (ranging from 34 fewer to 461 more). The evidence is limited by small sample sizes, few events, and wide confidence intervals. 5. Magnesium Sulfate for Inhibiting Preterm Labour: Very low-quality evidence suggests a potential reduction of 17 cases per 1,000 births, but the confidence intervals are wide (ranging from 26 fewer to 593 more). The evidence is further weakened by design limitations and small sample sizes. 6. Oxytocin Receptor Antagonists for Inhibiting Preterm Labour: Very low-quality evidence suggests an increase of 21 more cases per 1,000 births (ranging from 4 fewer to 92 more). The evidence is limited by design flaws and small sample sizes. 7. Nitric Oxide Donors for Inhibiting Preterm Labour: Low-quality evidence suggests an increase of 13 more cases per 1,000 births, but the confidence intervals are wide, ranging from 19 fewer to 49 more. The evidence is limited by design flaws and small sample sizes. 8. Progesterone Agents for Inhibiting Preterm Labour: Very low-quality evidence suggests a reduction of 2 cases per 1,000 births (ranging from 24 fewer to 335 more). The evidence is limited by small sample sizes, few events, and wide confidence intervals. 9. Relaxin for Inhibiting Preterm Labour: Very low-quality evidence suggests a reduction of 68 cases per 1,000 births (ranging from 272 fewer to 460 more). The evidence is limited by design flaws and small sample sizes. 10. Hydration for Inhibiting Preterm Labour: Very low-quality evidence suggests an increase of 11 more cases per 1,000 births. The evidence is limited by design flaws, small sample sizes, and wide confidence intervals. 11. Maintenance Therapy with Betamimetics: Low-quality evidence suggests an increase of 5 more cases per 1,000 births (ranging from 19 fewer to 49 more). The evidence is limited by design flaws and small sample sizes. 12. Maintenance Therapy with Magnesium: Very low-quality evidence suggests a reduction of 118 cases per 1,000 births (ranging from 308 fewer to 213 more). The evidence is limited by design flaws and small sample sizes. 13. Maintenance Therapy with Calcium Channel Blockers: Low-quality evidence suggests no pooled effect due to significant heterogeneity and design limitations in the contributing studies. 14. Maintenance Therapy with Oxytocin Antagonists: Very low-quality evidence suggests an increase of 13 fewer cases per 1,000 births (ranging from 44 fewer to 41 more). The evidence is limited by design flaws and small sample sizes. 15. General Limitations Across Studies: Many studies contributing data had significant design limitations, including small sample sizes, few events, and wide confidence intervals crossing the line of no effect. Statistical heterogeneity (I² > 60%) was frequently observed, indicating variability in the size and direction of effects across studies. Some estimates were based on single studies or studies with a high risk of bias, further limiting the reliability of the findings. In summary, while some interventions show promise in improving preterm birth outcomes, the overall quality of evidence is low to very low for most interventions. This highlights the need for further high-quality research to better understand the efficacy and safety of these interventions.
